title: Should IME composition be treated more explicitly as a distinct input context, rather than ordinary application shortcut input?

body:
### What is the issue with the HTML Standard?

## Background

When a user is in an IME composition session, they are not yet providing committed text. They are still in an uncommitted editing state: choosing candidates, confirming conversions, canceling them, or moving through candidate lists.

In practice, many web applications implement shortcuts such as Enter-to-submit, Tab-to-complete, Escape-to-close, or Arrow-key navigation on `keydown`. However, these same keys are also routinely used by IME users as part of ordinary text entry.
As a result, application shortcuts can interfere with composition and cause real problems such as accidental submission or disruption of text input.
Today, the burden is largely on every author to remember to special-case composition, even though composition is not an application shortcut context but part of the platform text input system. That feels backwards. [1][2]

There are already related UI Events discussions about composition-related key events and the meaning/timing of `isComposing`, including open issues in w3c/uievents on whether key events should be sent during composition and how `isComposing` behaves at composition completion. [3][4][5]

At the same time, composition-aware handling is not merely theoretical. Advanced web editors already need to treat composition as a special editing mode, because ordinary DOM updates, state synchronization, or plugin-driven input handling can interrupt or corrupt an active IME session.
For example, ProseMirror’s “composition overhaul” explicitly discusses avoiding decorations that interfere with the focused text node in order to prevent spurious interruptions of composition, and Slate has discussed handling composition code separately from ordinary `onKeyDown` / `onInput` flows for the same reason. [6][7]

## Problem

The practical web-platform model today seems to expose composition-time keyboard interaction too much like ordinary page-level shortcut input.

That means authors, including many who do not regularly use an IME themselves, often have to add defensive checks such as `isComposing` or browser-specific workarounds to avoid treating IME confirmation and candidate-navigation keys as application commands.
This is not just an implementation detail. It suggests that composition may not be modeled distinctly enough at the platform level, even though it is part of the text input system rather than ordinary shortcut handling.

## Question

Should IME composition be treated more explicitly as a distinct input context, rather than exposing composition-time keyboard operations to page script with largely the same practical semantics as ordinary application shortcut input?

I am not proposing a specific immediate mechanism here, and I am not claiming that this can simply be changed without compatibility consequences. Rather, I want to ask whether the current model is conceptually right.

## Related context:

+ [1] https://ef81sp.github.io/ime-vs-input-keyboard-shortcut/1
+ [2] https://kai-rin.github.io/your-form-submits-mid-japanese-input/
+ [3] https://github.com/w3c/uievents/issues/395
+ [4] https://github.com/w3c/uievents/issues/394
+ [5] https://github.com/w3c/input-events/issues/176
+ [6] https://discuss.prosemirror.net/t/composition-overhaul/1923
+ [7] https://github.com/ianstormtaylor/slate/issues/2578
